name: Tomas Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We do not sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers stay confidential; there is no right view here. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead percussion for touring theatre, from the quiet shaker to the big kettle drums called timpani. I also record short drum cues and coach two young players, and my music master’s helped me build a well paid reputation. I like the moment a whole cast lands on a beat together; loading a kit up a narrow stair after midnight wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What holds the household steady between tours?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a civil engineer, our children are grown, and we have fourteen months of expenses saved. I use an AI scheduling tool now and then, after the younger players have checked it, but I still compare every route with the actual train. The cues pay a quarter of my own music income, so I watch those orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead percussion for touring theatre shows, play the hard parts myself, and coach two younger drummers. In AI Plateau I would tell the band that a quicker route plan is useful, but nobody has cancelled a paid call. I sometimes use a scheduling tool, and I still check the venue's written times against the train timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The next tour is signed, my partner's engineering wage is steady, and we have fourteen months of expenses saved. One moved rehearsal is irritating, not a threat to the flat. I would worry more about a promoter cancelling the tour than about a little better software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week I will keep the signed tour, coaching calls, and equipment checks. In the first year of a small AI change I will compare each automated travel suggestion with the actual train and loading time before agreeing a new call. I will ask the tour manager to confirm any moved rehearsal fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this version. A computer can shorten my planning, but the kit still has to reach the theatre safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check the travel plan yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A route can look short on a map and still leave no time to unload the drums. An AI route planner does not carry a kettle drum up the old theatre stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one missed rehearsal cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be a nuisance rather than a household crisis with our current reserve. I would still ask for the contracted cancellation fee, because the junior players need their paid hours too.

say: I would welcome a **quicker route plan** while the paid tour remains booked.
I would check **written venue times** against the train timetable.
think: The **signed tour** and fourteen-month reserve cover a routine moved rehearsal.
My real worry is a **promoter cancellation**, not mild scheduling software.
do: Keep **signed calls** for touring and coaching, and inspect percussion gear through the mild first year.
Compare **tool travel suggestions** with real trains, loading time, and venue access before changing calls.
Request **written moved-rehearsal pay** from the tour manager.
feel: I feel **calm** because current paid work and savings absorb a normal schedule change.
fieldNote: He uses **occasional scheduling tools** already but checks practical transport and access himself.
His **calm** comes from a signed tour, partner wages, and a fourteen-month reserve.
S0.quote: An AI route planner does not carry a kettle drum up the old theatre stairs.

steps.text: Keep signed tour and coaching calls while inspecting percussion gear
Check automated travel suggestions against trains, loading time, and venue access
Request written fee before accepting a moved rehearsal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our touring players that Steady Disruption may replace the short drum cues I record, but it should not turn a live rehearsal into a free download. I would ask our players' association to show minimum fees for recorded reuse and paid setup time. I would test a new audio checker on my own practice take before asking anyone else to trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recorded cues bring about a quarter of my own musician pay. I expect that share to shrink while the touring dates still need a human drummer, and fourteen months saved buys time rather than another buyer. I do not want the junior player doing unpaid fixes for a cheaper software score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will ask the sound engineer to teach me a new AI stem checker, which compares separate recorded instrument parts, using only my own nameless practice take. I will trial it only after the manager approves a theatre-funded paid-use licence, local storage and a paid lesson for both of us outside booked calls. I will play the result against the original beat and keep cast recordings private; I will stop if it misses notes or leaks a file. In the first disruption year I will keep the signed tour and bring actual setup hours and cue contracts to the players’ association for a written fee proposal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the cue quarter, but I can still take paid calls and test a tool before using it. An orange warning on a screen is not proof that the drummer played the wrong beat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the new checker useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to catch a misplaced beat that I can hear when I play the take back. A neat display that misses the drum entrance wastes paid editing time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the association?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the two cue invoices and the tour sheet with setup hours. A fee table based on those numbers is easier to bargain over than saying technology is unfair.

say: Recorded **drum cues** may lose buyers while the live tour still pays its players.
I would ask for **paid setup and reuse** terms using actual cue invoices.
think: A **quarter of pay** from cues could shrink before my stage chair does.
A **fourteen-month reserve** buys time, not permanent replacement orders.
do: Learn **AI stem checker** after funded paid-use licence/local approval and paid off-call lesson; use own nameless take, manually compare beats/protect cast files.
Keep **signed tour calls** in the first disruption year and stop the checker for errors or leaks.
Bring **cue invoices** and setup hours to the players' association for written pay and reuse terms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about cue losses, with enough paid work and savings to test carefully.
fieldNote: The **new checker trial** is genuine learning, with owned material, manual comparison, and privacy limits.
His **association proposal** uses actual invoices and setup hours rather than a broad technology claim.
S1.quote: An orange warning on a screen is not proof that the drummer played the wrong beat.

steps.text: Learn AI checker after funded licence/local approval and paid off-call lesson; manually compare own nameless take
Bring cue invoices and setup hours to players’ association for paid reuse terms
Stop AI checker for wrong notes or file leaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2028 could end short cue orders while we still play live shows until capable stage robots arrive around 2031. I would show junior players the signed call sheet, because a lost recording order is not a reason to erase a paid rehearsal. I would ask the association to count actual cancelled cue fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my cue quarter to disappear by 2028. The signed tour, partner wage, and fourteen-month reserve make that painful but manageable for a while. If live shows also closed, the problem would be much larger, but I am not calling that my forecast for the thinking-AI year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will request an actual pension estimate and keep the signed tour and coaching dates. I will ask the association to document lost cue orders and bargain for payment when old takes are reused. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028 I will set the cue line to zero in our household budget and take any extra theatre setup only when a written fee covers my time and travel, without cancelling already paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the expected quarter loss, not certain that my live job ends. Fourteen months saved gives me a search window, not an excuse to make my junior colleagues work for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why request the pension figure now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 I want to know the actual amount before deciding how long touring must continue. The reserve is money for bills, not proof that a pension will cover them at 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy new equipment to replace the lost cue work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not on a guess that venues will rent it. I would first ask whether anyone has a paid contract and a place to store the gear safely.

say: Short **cue orders** may end in 2028, three years before capable stage robots arrive.
I would protect **paid rehearsal calls** even when recording buyers disappear.
think: I expect a **quarter of musician pay** from cues to vanish in 2028.
A **live-show closure** would be worse, but I have not made it my forecast.
do: Request **actual pension estimate** and keep signed tour and coaching dates this month.
Ask the **players' association** to log lost cue orders and bargain for old-take reuse pay.
Budget **zero cue income** after 2028; accept extra paid setup only with written time and travel fees.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected cue loss, with paid calls and savings still giving me options.
fieldNote: The **cue quarter** is the expected loss; a live-show closure remains conditional.
He asks for **pension facts** and refuses equipment spending without real paid demand.
S2.quote: The reserve is money for bills, not proof that a pension will cover them at 68.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and keep signed tour and coaching dates
Ask players’ association to document lost cue orders and bargain for reuse pay
Budget zero cue income after 2028; accept extra setup only for written time and travel pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to test whether local theatres will pay to rent a percussion kit, while stage robots come around 2034. I would publish a rental price only after the theatres confirm real dates and insurance terms. This would be a separate equipment business, not a way to make our tour rehearsal unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know two small theatres that borrow drums now, but a friendly request is not a signed hire. Cue fees could fade before 2031, and a paid rental line might help if the numbers cover the kit, cleaning, and my setup time. I will not raid the household reserve to buy shiny drums for imaginary customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask for two signed paid rental dates that cover the kit cost across the first season, insurance, cleaning, setup time, and transport. Only then would I buy a spare kit from cash above our twelve-month household reserve. In the first year after 2031 I will inspect each drum before collection, replace or refund unsafe equipment, renew rentals only at the same full-cost floor, keep the booked tour calls, and request the actual pension estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about cue work, yet five years gives me time to check demand before spending. A signed hire date is more useful than ten people saying a spare drum kit sounds clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if one theatre signs and the other only talks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait, because one fee does not repay the kit and its insurance while protecting our reserve. The two signed dates have to cover the purchase over that first season and still pay for my labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a damaged kit before pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would inspect and repair it before anyone loads it, and I would not send it out unsafe. If I cannot provide a safe replacement, the renter gets the whole hire payment back.

say: I would offer a **separate drum-kit rental** only after paid dates and insurance are written.
The **2034 robot date** is later than thinking AGI in 2031.
think: The **cue market** may fade before 2031, making a second income line worth testing.
Our **household reserve** should not buy equipment without two full-cost paid hires.
do: Secure **two written paid rentals** covering kit, insurance, cleaning, setup, and transport before buying.
Use **cash above twelve months** of household reserve for any spare kit purchase.
Inspect **each kit**; replace or fully refund unsafe gear, renew after 2031 at full cost, keep tour calls, and request pension estimate.
feel: I feel **anxious** about cues, with enough warning to test a paid rental line.
fieldNote: His **second income** is equipment rental, funded only after two paid contracts cover every material cost.
The **safety fallback** is a safe replacement or full refund, at launch and renewal.
S3.quote: A signed hire date is more useful than ten people saying a spare drum kit sounds clever.

steps.text: Get two signed kit rentals covering purchase, insurance, cleaning, setup, and transport
Buy spare kit only from cash above twelve-month household reserve
Inspect each rental; replace or fully refund unsafe kit; renew only at full-cost floor
Keep booked tour calls and request actual pension estimate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the touring players that AGI by 2036 leaves time to protect paid calls, while capable stage robots follow around 2039. A drum can be copied on a screen sooner than a theatre can load one safely. I would keep junior players' setup pay written into the tour agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our paid tour and fourteen-month reserve secure the near term, but the cue quarter could thin well before 2036. I might still want to play at 68; I cannot promise a retirement date without the actual pension amount and a calendar that pays. The grown children have their own households, so I do not count their wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will request the actual pension estimate and keep the signed tour and coaching calendar. I will save ten percent of each cleared show fee above the twelve-month reserve floor for a later work gap, after band wages and bills are paid. In the first year after 2036 I will keep taking paid theatre calls and use the association's written setup fee; I will reduce touring only if pension payments are confirmed payable for that period and other signed earnings cover our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy because the next tours are paid and there is time to plan, though cue buyers may leave. A calendar with empty boxes is not a pension plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you slow down when the first robot drummer arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at my hands, the signed calls, and the pension statement, not only the robot. If I can still play well and the job pays, I may keep touring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who protects the junior players' fees if you cut dates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their setup hours must remain in the written agreement whether I play or another leader takes the chair. I would bring the rate sheet to the association meeting before giving up a date.

say: I would keep **junior setup fees** written into touring agreements through the decade.
The **2039 stage-robot date** follows thinking AGI in 2036 by about three years.
think: Current **tour pay and reserves** secure the next seasons, not an unknown retirement income.
The **cue quarter** may shrink before 2036 even if stage work lasts longer.
do: Request **actual pension estimate** and keep signed tour and coaching calls this month.
Save **ten percent** of cleared show fees above a twelve-month reserve after band wages and bills.
Keep **paid post-2036 calls** with association setup rates; reduce touring only when verified payable pension and signed earnings cover costs.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later cue sales while signed tours and savings support us now.
fieldNote: His **near-term security** comes from signed touring pay and fourteen months saved.
A **slower touring calendar** needs actual pension and other signed earnings covering household bills.
S4.quote: A calendar with empty boxes is not a pension plan.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and keep signed tour and coaching calls
Save ten percent of cleared show fees after band wages and bills above twelve-month floor
Keep written junior setup rates through association agreement
Keep paid post-2036 calls; slow only if verified payable pension and earnings cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the cue quarter could vanish before I know what equipment hires or extra live work really pay. A signed tour, an actual pension estimate, and written fees for the junior players would help. I can afford to test a second line later, but I will not use the household reserve as applause money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the stairs before the drums arrive. A theatre pays for a sound, but the people lifting the kit need time, wages, and a safe doorway.

headlineQuote: A theatre pays for a sound, but the people lifting the kit need time, wages, and a safe doorway.
portrait: Tomas is a **58-year-old** senior touring percussion leader with a music master’s, short cue orders, and two coached players.
A partner wage and **fourteen-month reserve** support a well paid household calendar.
He uses **occasional scheduling AI** and checks travel against trains and venue loading time.
He tests **drum-kit rental** only after signed hires cover purchase and running costs above the household reserve.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end cue fees worth a quarter of his own music pay before another paid line is proven.
whatWouldHelp: A **signed tour**, actual pension estimate, and written junior setup fees would protect choices and earnings.
